article.title: As birds migrate south, there's an invisible danger: glass
article.summary: Every migration season, huge numbers of birds die when they fly into glass buildings they can't see. The story follows volunteers who walk a set route through Washington, DC each morning to find fallen birds before they are lost. It also looks at a night in Chicago when a convention center's glass wall killed close to a thousand birds. Birding groups, government agencies and others are now joining forces to tackle the problem together.
facts: Researchers estimate that at least a billion birds die from building collisions in the U.S. every year.
On one October night in 2023, nearly a thousand migrating birds were found dead at a single Chicago convention center.
Volunteers with Lights Out DC walk the same route every morning in migration season to find dead or injured birds before rats or custodians do.
Reflections in glass strongly attract birds, and some buildings funnel them toward a tall glass wall.
questions: Why might a bird's migration instincts fail to prepare it for modern glass architecture?
How should cities balance attractive glass buildings against the toll on wildlife?
What small changes could you make at your own home or workplace to help migrating birds?

related.t: Crash land home for the holidays (Columbia Climate School, State of the Planet)

alt.title: New Tracking Technology Reveals Hidden Animal Migration Routes
alt.summary: Decades of satellite-collar data on Wyoming's deer, elk and pronghorn are being used to map migration corridors across the state. Scientists capture animals from helicopters and fit them with collars that record where the herds go. The collars revealed an overlooked route that was rare within its herd and would have been blocked if a key property had been developed. A conservation fund bought the land and turned it into a wildlife habitat management area.
facts: Migration routes can be hard to find because they may be used by only a small part of a herd.
Researchers rely on the fact that animals tend to return to the same habitats year after year.
Biologists capture deer from helicopters to fit them with tracking collars.
One newly mapped route was saved when conservationists raised money to buy the land along it.
questions: If a migration route is used by only a few animals, how much protection does it deserve?
What are the trade-offs between collaring wild animals and the knowledge we gain from it?
How might a route you never knew existed change decisions about building roads or housing?

article.title: Experts uncover a truly bizarre prehistoric animal – with teeth like a seal, a platypus-like pelvis and the tail of an otter
article.summary: Researchers have described Megacauda, a mammal-like animal that lived over 160 million years ago and combined traits now found in very different animals. Micro-CT scans let the team rebuild its skull and skeleton in detail. Small bony projections on the roof of its mouth and specialised throat bones suggest it already had parts of the machinery mammals use to suckle and swallow. The find pushes back the timeline for how a defining mammal feeding habit evolved.
facts: Its cheek teeth were blade-like, much like a modern seal's.
Its pelvis resembled a platypus's, and its tail looked like an otter's.
Throat bones called hyoids help anchor the swallowing muscles of living mammals, and this animal had specialised ones.
Soft-tissue features like these are rarely preserved in fossils, so scientists had long struggled to date them.
questions: Why might the ability to swallow milk safely have mattered so much for early mammal relatives?
How can scientists infer soft tissues like muscles from bones alone, and how reliable are those inferences?
What does a mix of seal, platypus and otter traits tell us about how evolution recombines body features?

related.t: Mammals’ weird way of swallowing is at least 165 million years old (NOVA)
A bone that aids chewing may have helped start the Age of Mammals (Science News)

alt.title: 6-Million-Year-Old Bizarre Whale Swam Ancient Oceans With Nostrils on One Side of Its Face
alt.summary: Scientists have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose skull was so crooked that both nostrils ended up on its left side. Lopsided skulls are normal in sperm whales because of their echolocation and sound-making organs, but this one goes much further. Its neck joints suggest it could tilt its head sharply downward. Together with dense bone and a downturned snout, that would have let it cruise just above the seabed and feed near the sediment.
facts: Both of its nostrils sat on the left side of its face.
Its neck joints suggest it could bend its head down by as much as 55 degrees.
It lived off the coast of what is now Peru and Mexico in the Late Miocene, around six million years ago.
Dense skull bone helped it stay low over the seafloor while it fed.
questions: Why might a lopsided skull be an advantage for an animal that hunts using sound?
How do scientists work out how an extinct animal moved or fed from its skull and neck bones?
What other living animals have asymmetric bodies, and what might drive that?

related.t: Extreme cranial asymmetry in extinct benthic feeding sperm whales (Communications Biology)
Scaphokogia huachafo - A Bizarre Late Miocene Toothed Whale

article.title: Twins are a mirror to each other – and a window into the mysteries of genetics
article.summary: Psychologist Nancy Segal explains why twins are so useful to geneticists. Identical twins share all their genes, so comparing them with fraternal twins shows how much a trait is down to genes. The most revealing cases are identical twins raised apart. She describes studying two pairs of Colombian twins who were reunited as adults, and finding that their personalities lined up closely with their genetic twins rather than with the families who raised them.
facts: Identical twins form when one fertilized egg divides within about the first 14 days after conception.
If identical twins raised apart are as alike as identical twins raised together, that is stronger evidence that genes matter.
Segal travelled to Bogotá to study two sets of Colombian identical twins, one pair from the city and one from the countryside.

One of the Colombian pairs was outgoing and risk-taking, and the reunited twins' personalities matched almost perfectly with their genetic twins. Other coverage says the two pairs had been accidentally swapped at birth and raised as if they were fraternal twins.
questions: If identical twins raised apart turn out strikingly alike, what does that say about how much of who we are is decided before birth?
What ethical rules should apply when researchers study twins who were separated, whether by accident or on purpose?
Why might it be misleading to treat coincidences between reunited twins as proof that genes control behaviour?

related.t: Twin Studies Expert Nancy Segal Featured in Netflix Documentary 'The Accidental Twins' (Cal State Fullerton)

alt.title: Unique twin study sheds new light on TBI and risk of cognitive decline
alt.summary: Researchers used a registry of World War II veteran twins to ask whether a head injury in early adulthood affects thinking decades later. By comparing identical twins where only one had a traumatic brain injury, they could largely hold genes and upbringing constant. The injured twins tended to score lower on cognitive tests at about age 70. Outside experts called the twin design a real strength of the study.
facts: The study drew on 8,662 men born between 1917 and 1927 who were in a national twin registry.
It included 589 pairs of identical twins where only one twin had a brain injury.
Injuries that knocked someone unconscious, or that happened after age 24, were linked to a bigger drop in thinking skills.
An outside neurologist said this was one of the first, if not the first, studies of this question to use a twin design.
questions: How does comparing identical twins let researchers separate the effect of an accident from the effect of genes?
What might people who have 'fully recovered' from a concussion do differently if they knew about long-term risks?
What are the limits of relying on injuries that participants remember and report themselves?

related.t: Concussions Cause Greater Cognitive Declines in Later Life (Duke Psychiatry)
Concussions Early in Life Tied to Late Life Cognitive Decline (American Academy of Neurology)

article.title: 7 Times A.I. Helped Unlock Ancient Secrets
article.summary: This roundup looks at how artificial intelligence is helping scholars read texts from the ancient world. One case is a neural network that translates parts of Mesopotamian clay tablets from Akkadian into English. Others include AI help with piecing together the Epic of Gilgamesh and student contests to read carbonized Herculaneum scrolls. The article shows that machine translation can work on languages that disappeared thousands of years ago, not only on living ones.
facts: In May 2023, researchers from two Israeli universities trained a neural network to translate parts of cuneiform tablets from Akkadian into English.
One sample line the system produced says that a man who keeps his clothes clean will have long days.
The researchers admit that ancient languages are hard to translate because only fragments of the texts survive.
They say future progress depends on digitizing more existing texts to use as training data.
questions: What does a machine translator lose when the only texts it can learn from are fragments of a dead language?
Should AI translations of ancient texts be treated as a first draft for experts, or can they be trusted on their own?
How does translating a language no one has spoken for 2,000 years differ from translating a modern language like French?

related.t: Translating Akkadian to English with neural machine translation
New AI translates 5,000-year-old cuneiform tablets instantly

alt.title: The Perpetual Quest for a Truth Machine
alt.summary: This feature follows the long human dream of handing off thinking and language to a machine. It starts with the 13th-century philosopher Ramon Llull, who built paper wheels of basic concepts. He believed they could prove religious truths to doubters and end arguments. The story then follows later thinkers such as Leibniz, who admired the idea but found it lacking, and who wanted a precise language that could settle disputes by calculation. It reads as a prehistory of today's language-handling AI.
facts: Llull's paper wheels were labeled with concepts such as goodness, eternity, understanding and love.
Llull claimed his machine could prove the existence of the Christian God even to a stubborn heretic.
His detailed examples ended up hiding how the machine actually worked, and he did not win the converts he hoped for.
Leibniz was inspired by Llull's system, and the idea of a universal language that reduces reasoning to calculation traces partly back to Llull.
questions: Why have people for so long wanted a machine that could settle arguments by working with language?
Is a universal language that removes misunderstanding possible, or would it lose something important about human speech?
How are today's language models similar to, and different from, Llull's paper wheels?

related.t: Thinking Machines: Ramon Llull and the ars combinatoria (EPFL)
